Hands-on Exercise 7

Modelling Geographical Accessibility

Author

An Loc

Published

13 Oct 2026

Modified

16 Oct 2026

1 Overview

In Exercise 6, townships were grouped into regions by the similarity of their ICT rates. In this exercise, accessibility is measured for every part of Singapore: how easily the residents of each part can reach one of the 120 eldercare centres in the government’s list of eldercare services.

On slide 3, accessibility is “the measure of the capacity of a location to be reached from, or to be reached by, different locations”, the definition of Rodrigue et al. (2013). Every measure in this exercise combines demand, supply and the cost of travel:

  • the demand at each place, the number of people who may use the service;
  • the supply at each service location, the amount of service available;
  • the cost of travel between each place and each service location, here the network distance along the roads.

Part 1 is a reproduction of r4gdsa chapter 17, which computes three measures with the ac() function of the SpatialAcc package: Hansen’s potential model, the kernel density two-step floating catchment area method (KD2SFCA) and the spatial accessibility measure (SAM). In Part 2, the output of ac() is compared with the formulas on the Lesson 7 slides and in the readings, and the distance matrix is checked. The 2SFCA and E2SFCA methods of slides 24 to 28 are added, and the constant demand of the chapter is replaced with the number of residents aged 65 and over.

NoteSources

The hands-on exercise for Lesson 7 is this chapter:

The Lesson 7 outline lists four readings for before the lesson.

Reading What it contributes Used in
Long (2017), “Modelling Accessibility”, GIS&T Body of Knowledge Network space and network distance; four classes of accessibility measure; the remark that gravity-based measures have no clear definition of a high or low value, so “all analysis must be relative”; aggregation of accessibility to regions 3.1, 4.1, 4.6
Hansen (1959), Accessibility and Residential Growth Accessibility as the sum of the opportunities at each zone divided by the separation raised to an exponent, and exponents of 2.2 to 3.0 by trip purpose 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 4.2, 4.3
Luo and Wang (2003), “Measures of spatial accessibility to health care in a GIS environment” The two steps of 2SFCA; 2SFCA as a special case of the gravity model with competition; the population-weighted mean of the accessibility scores equals the ratio of total supply to total demand; a larger catchment gives smoother scores 3.1, 3.2, 3.4, 4.2 to 4.6
Luo and Qi (2009), “An enhanced two-step floating catchment area (E2SFCA) method” Three travel zones within the catchment, with weights from a Gaussian function 4.2 to 4.6

The outline links Hansen (1959) to a PDF at MIT. The PDF is Hansen’s master’s thesis of 1959, which contains the accessibility model and the exponents used on this page. The article named on the outline, “How Accessibility Shapes Land Use”, is a summary of the thesis, published in the Journal of the American Institute of Planners in 1959.

Of the six references the outline also lists, the following are used on this page:

Reference What it contributes Used in
Polzin, Borges and Coelho (2014), “An extended kernel density two-step floating catchment area method” KD2SFCA as defined by Dai and Wang (2011), with the Epanechnikov kernel 3.2, 4.2 to 4.5
Cheng et al. (2016), “Spatial difference analysis for accessibility to high level hospitals based on travel time in Shenzhen, China” KD2SFCA with a Gaussian kernel whose width is set so that the weight at the catchment edge is 0.05 3.2, 4.2 to 4.5
Rodrigue, Comtois and Slack (2013), The Geography of Transport Systems, “Transportation and Accessibility” The definition of accessibility quoted on slide 3 1

Rich (1980) and Orpana and Lampinen (2003) cover potential models and spatial choice models in general, as background reading for this page.

Slide 29 cites Kalogirou and Foley (2006) for SAM. The paper is cited on slide 29 only, and is used in sections 3.1, 3.3, 3.4, 4.1 to 4.3 and 4.5. Its first author wrote the SpatialAcc package.

The outline’s “All About R” section links three packages. SpatialAcc is used throughout. The potential package (Stewart’s potential model) and the accessibility package compute families of measure that SpatialAcc also computes. This page uses only SpatialAcc.

The Lesson 7 slide deck is dated 12 October 2026, with 29 numbered slides. Slide 2 lists the Stewart and Hansen potential models, 2SFCA, KD2SFCA and SAM. Slides 19 and 20 give the formula of Stewart’s potential model. Slides 24 to 27 give the formulas of 2SFCA and E2SFCA, and slide 29 gives the formula of SAM. The deck has no formula for the Hansen model or for KD2SFCA.

2.3 Geospatial data

2.3.1 Reading the three layers

The three layers have separate roles in the computation of Part 1:

Object Layer One feature is Used for
hexagons hexagons a hexagon of the main island, Jurong Island or Sentosa demand in ac() (section 2.3.3) and rows of the distance matrix (section 2.4); unit of the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM scores (sections 3.1 to 3.3)
eldercare ELDERCARE an eldercare service, with its postal code and address supply in ac() (section 2.3.3) and columns of the distance matrix (section 2.4); red points on the maps of sections 3.1.2, 3.2.2 and 3.3.2
mpsz MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL a subzone of the URA Master Plan 2014, with its planning area and region region of each hexagon, for the boxplots of sections 3.1.3, 3.2.3 and 3.3.3 
mpsz <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                layer = "MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL")
hexagons <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                    layer = "hexagons")
eldercare <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial",
                     layer = "ELDERCARE")
tibble(layer = c("mpsz", "hexagons", "eldercare"),
       features = c(nrow(mpsz), nrow(hexagons), nrow(eldercare)),
       geometry = c(as.character(st_geometry_type(mpsz, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(hexagons, by_geometry = FALSE)),
                    as.character(st_geometry_type(eldercare, by_geometry = FALSE))),
       epsg = c(st_crs(mpsz)$epsg, st_crs(hexagons)$epsg, st_crs(eldercare)$epsg)) |>
  kable()
layer features geometry epsg
mpsz 323 MULTIPOLYGON NA
hexagons 3125 POLYGON 3414
eldercare 120 POINT 3414
NoteHow the code works 
st_read(dsn, layer)                                       # sf
st_geometry_type(x, by_geometry = FALSE)                  # sf
st_crs(x)$epsg                                            # sf
tibble(...)                                               # tibble
kable(x, digits)                                          # knitr
  • st_read() reads the shapefile named by layer from the folder dsn into a simple feature data frame. results: hide suppresses the report that st_read() prints for each file.
  • st_geometry_type(by_geometry = FALSE) returns one geometry type for the whole layer.
  • st_crs()$epsg returns the EPSG code of the coordinate reference system, or NA when the file does not contain one.
  • tibble() builds a data frame from vectors of equal length, one column for each argument. Here the table has one row for each layer.
  • kable() prints a data frame as a formatted table. The other tables on this page are also printed with kable(). Where digits is given, it rounds the numbers.

The subzones have no EPSG code: their projection file describes SVY21 by its parameters only. The hexagons and the eldercare centres are already in SVY21 with EPSG code 3414.

The map below shows the hexagons, the subzone boundaries and the eldercare centres together.

tm_borders(col, lwd)                                      # tmap
tm_dots(fill, size)                                       # tmap
tm_add_legend(type, labels, fill, col)                    # tmap
  • Each tm_shape() starts a layer, and the layers are drawn in order: the hexagons in grey with white borders, the subzone boundaries in blue, and the centres as red points.
  • The extent and the coordinate reference system of the map are those of the first layer, hexagons. The subzones are in the same SVY21 projection as the hexagons, so the two layers line up although the EPSG code of the subzones is added only in section 2.3.2.

Five subzones have no hexagon: the North-Eastern Islands (Pulau Ubin and Pulau Tekong), Pulau Seletar, Sudong, Semakau and the Southern Group. Of the 120 centres, 61 are in the Central Region, which has 136 km² of the 781 km² of land in the subzone layer. The West Region, with 257 km², has 20 centres.

2.3.2 Coordinate reference system

mpsz <- st_transform(mpsz, 3414)
eldercare <- st_transform(eldercare, 3414)
hexagons <- st_transform(hexagons, 3414)

st_crs(mpsz)$epsg
[1] 3414
NoteHow the code works 
st_transform(x, crs)                                      # sf
  • st_transform() converts the coordinates of x to the coordinate reference system crs, here EPSG:3414, SVY21 / Singapore TM. For hexagons and eldercare, which are already in EPSG:3414, the call changes nothing. For mpsz, the call keeps the SVY21 projection and adds the EPSG code.

The chapter text names the subzone layer MP14_SUBZONE_WEB_PL and the transformed object mpsz_svy21. The chapter’s code reads the layer MP14_SUBZONE_NO_SEA_PL into the object mpsz.

TipHexagons as the spatial unit

On slides 9 to 11, hexagons are the spatial unit. Administrative units such as subzones have shapes and sizes set by planning decisions. Every hexagon has the same area. Of the regular polygons that tile a plane, the hexagon is the closest to a circle.

Each hexagon covers 216,506 m². Its sides are 288.7 m long, and the distance from its centre to the middle of each side is 250 m. The “250m radius” of section 17.2 is that distance. The centres of two neighbouring hexagons are 500 m apart.

The hexagons are the units of demand in every measure on this page. The demand of a hexagon is placed at its centre point. The distance to each eldercare centre is measured from that point.

2.3.3 Demand and capacity

The layers read in section 2.3.1 have no field for the demand of a hexagon or the capacity of a centre. The code below adds a demand column to hexagons and a capacity column to eldercare. It also keeps only the identifier fid of hexagons and eldercare, and the postal code of each centre.

eldercare <- eldercare |>
  select(fid, ADDRESSPOS) |>
  mutate(capacity = 100)

hexagons <- hexagons |>
  select(fid) |>
  mutate(demand = 100)
NoteHow the code works 
select(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
mutate(.data, ...)                                        # dplyr
  • select() keeps the identifier fid of each layer, and the postal code of each centre. The geometry column is kept by sf without being named.
  • mutate() adds a constant column to each layer: a capacity of 100 for each centre, and a demand of 100 for each hexagon.

In the chapter, the same value is used for every hexagon and every centre “for the purpose of this hands-on exercise”, with a note that the actual demand and capacity should be used in practice. The ELDERCARE layer has no field on the size of a centre, so the capacity stays at 100 on this page. With the same demand in every hexagon and the same capacity at every centre, the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM scores depend only on the distances in the distance matrix.

NoteHow the code works 
read_csv(file, skip)                                      # readr
glimpse(x)                                                # dplyr
  • read_csv() reads the file into a tibble. With the default skip = 0, reading starts at the first line.
  • glimpse() prints the number of rows and columns, and the type and first values of each column.

The file has one row per pair of hexagon and eldercare centre: 3,125 hexagons × 120 centres = 375,000 rows.

TipFields of the distance matrix

Each row gives the cost of travel, in metres, from the centre of one hexagon to one eldercare centre, divided into these parts:

Field Distance
entry_cost from the centre of the hexagon to the nearest road
network_cost along the road network
exit_cost from the road to the eldercare centre
total_cost the sum of entry_cost, network_cost and exit_cost

The invented street map below draws the entry_cost, network_cost and exit_cost of one pair of hexagon and centre as three coloured lines.

The table shows the first three rows of the file, which give the distances from hexagon 1 to the first three centres.

origin_id destination_id entry_cost network_cost exit_cost total_cost
1 1 667.9 19846.9 47.6 20562.5
1 2 667.9 45026.8 31.9 45726.6
1 3 667.9 17644.2 173.5 18485.6

Kalogirou and Foley (2006), the source of SAM, computed their distances in the same three parts: from the centroid of each district to the nearest node of the road network, along the network, and from the network to the hospital. Long (2017, section 2.2) gives the reason for distances along the network: “most human movement occurs along a spatial network consisting of roads, railways, and paths”. Slide 6 shows the straight-line (“Cartesian”) distance and the network distance of the same trip.

2.4.2 From long to wide

ODMatrix has one row for each pair of hexagon and eldercare centre. ac() takes a matrix with one row for each hexagon and one column for each centre. The chapter’s code uses spread(), with a note that pivot_wider() has replaced it since tidyr 1.0.

distmat <- ODMatrix |>
  select(origin_id, destination_id, total_cost) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = destination_id,
              values_from = total_cost)

c(rows_match = identical(distmat$origin_id, hexagons$fid),
  cols_match = identical(as.numeric(names(distmat)[-1]),
                         as.numeric(eldercare$fid)))
rows_match cols_match 
      TRUE       TRUE
NoteHow the code works 
pivot_wider(data, names_from, values_from)                # tidyr
identical(x, y)                                           # base R
  • select() keeps the three columns needed: the hexagon, the centre and the total distance.
  • pivot_wider() makes one column for each value of destination_id, named by that value, and fills it with the total_cost of each hexagon to that centre. The result has one row for each origin_id.
  • identical() checks that the rows are in the order of hexagons$fid, and that the column names are in the order of eldercare$fid.

In the invented example below, two hexagons and three centres make six pairs of hexagon and centre, one row each. Each centre has its own colour. pivot_wider() places each value in the column of its centre and the row of its hexagon.

ODMatrix before the code has one row for each pair of hexagon and centre, 375,000 rows. The columns that select() keeps are shaded. The distance from hexagon 1 to centre 2 is in bold:

origin_id destination_id entry_cost network_cost exit_cost total_cost
1 1 667.9 19,846.9 47.6 20,562.5
1 2 667.9 45,026.8 31.9 45,726.6
1 3 667.9 17,644.2 173.5 18,485.6
… … … … … …
2 1 716.4 22,304.9 47.6 23,069.0
2 2 716.4 47,484.8 31.9 48,233.1
2 3 716.4 20,102.2 173.5 20,992.1
… … … … … …

distmat after the code has one row for each hexagon, 3,125 rows, and 121 columns: origin_id and one column for each of the 120 centres. The distance from hexagon 1 to centre 2 is in row 1, column 2:

origin_id 1 2 3 … 133
1 20,562.5 45,726.6 18,485.6 … 22,919.6
2 23,069.0 48,233.1 20,992.1 … 25,426.2
… … … … … …

identical() compares two vectors position by position, and returns TRUE only when every position holds the same value. The table shows the first positions of the column names of distmat and of eldercare$fid.

1st 2nd 3rd 4th 5th 6th 7th …
column names of distmat 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 …
eldercare$fid 1 2 3 4 5 6 8 …
the same names sorted as text 1 10 100 101 103 104 105 …

The column names of distmat and eldercare$fid are the same at every position, so identical() returns TRUE. If the columns had been sorted as text, identical() would return FALSE, because of the bold values. Then ac() would pair the second column, centre 10, with the capacity of centre 2.

ac() matches the matrix to the demand and the capacity by position: row \(i\) to the \(i\)-th hexagon, column \(j\) to the \(j\)-th centre. The chapter’s code includes no check of the order. The row check and the column check return TRUE, so the rows of distmat follow the order of hexagons and the columns follow the order of eldercare.

The 120 centres have identifiers between 1 and 133, with gaps. The columns of distmat follow the order of the identifiers. After the first gap, the fid of the \(j\)-th centre is larger than \(j\).

The first column of distmat holds origin_id. The column is removed, and the distances are converted from metres to kilometres:

distmat <- distmat |>
  select(-origin_id)

distmat_km <- as.matrix(distmat / 1000)
dim(distmat_km)
[1] 3125  120
NoteHow the code works 
as.matrix(x)                                              # base R
  • select(-origin_id) drops the identifier column. In the chapter’s code, the same step is select(c(-c('origin_id'))).
  • Dividing the tibble by 1000 converts every distance from metres to kilometres. as.matrix() converts the result to a numeric matrix of 3,125 rows and 120 columns.
  • ac() converts its argument D to a matrix in the first line of its source (section 4.2), so ac() gives the same scores for the tibble as for the matrix. The matrix is needed in sections 4.3 and 4.4, where the distances are multiplied with %*%, which takes only matrices.

According to the chapter, “the distance is measured in metre because SVY21 projected coordinate system is used”. The distances are along roads. Their unit comes from the network analysis that produced the file. The conversion to kilometres changes the scores, because the Hansen and KD2SFCA formulas in ac() raise e to a power of the distance (section 4.2): the same distance gives a different weight in metres than in kilometres.

3 Part 1: Chapter 17

This part follows r4gdsa Chapter 17, sections 17.6 to 17.8. The Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures are each computed with ac(), joined to the hexagons, mapped, and compared across the five regions of the Master Plan.

3.1 Hansen’s potential model

TipThe potential model of Hansen (1959)

Hansen (1959) defines accessibility as “the potential of opportunities for interaction”. The definition comes from Stewart’s potential of population (slide 19). Hansen describes that potential as “directly proportional to the size of the group (activity level) and inversely proportional to the distance or separation from that group”. In Hansen’s formula, the accessibility of zone \(i\) is a sum over all zones \(j\). In this exercise, zone \(i\) is a hexagon and zone \(j\) is an eldercare centre:

\[A_i = \sum_j \frac{S_j}{T_{ij}^{\,x}} = \sum_j \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{(\text{road distance from hexagon } i \text{ to centre } j)^{x}}\]

\(x\) is an exponent of distance. The contribution of a centre to the score of a hexagon increases with the capacity of the centre and decreases with the distance between the centre and the hexagon. A larger \(x\) makes the contribution decrease faster with distance. In the speaker notes of slide 7, the power function is traced to Newton’s law of gravitation, the origin of the term gravity model. According to the same notes, \(x\) is large for grocery shopping, because people travel only a short distance for groceries. For furniture shopping, \(x\) is small, because people travel farther than for groceries. The formula has no catchment, so every centre adds to the score of every hexagon, at any distance.

The example below has one hexagon and three centres, with \(x = 2\). The distances and capacities are invented for this example. A line joins the hexagon to each centre. A wider line marks a larger term \(S_j/T_{ij}^2\).

Centre B is twice as far from the hexagon as centre A, so its term is a quarter of the term of centre A. Centre C is as far from the hexagon as centre B and has four times the capacity of centre B, so the term of centre C is four times the term of centre B, the same as the term of centre A.

Slide 8 shows two forms of distance decay: the power function \(\alpha / d^{\beta}\) and the exponential function \(\alpha e^{-\beta d}\). Hansen (1959, p. 5) uses the power function, which is \(1/d^2\) with \(x = 2\). The SpatialAcc manual describes power as “the power of the separation variable”. The source of ac(), printed in section 4.2, computes the exponential function: with power = 2, the value in the chapter’s code, the weight is \(e^{-2d}\), where \(d\) is the road distance in kilometres. The table compares the weights of \(1/d^2\) and \(e^{-2d}\), each relative to the weight of a centre 1 km away:

Function Formula 1 km 2 km 4 km 8 km Rule
Hansen (1959), \(x = 2\) \(1/d^2\) 1 \(1/4\) \(1/16\) \(1/64\) divided by 4 each time the distance doubles
ac(), power = 2 \(e^{-2d}\) 1 \(1/7\) \(1/403\) \(1/1{,}202{,}604\) divided by \(e^2 = 7.4\) for each extra kilometre

The weight of the power function depends on the ratio of two distances, and the weight of the exponential function on their difference.

3.1.1 Hansen scores from ac()

The distance matrix holds 375,000 road distances, one for each pair of hexagon and centre. The code in this section turns them into one Hansen score for each of the 3,125 hexagons, and adds the scores to the hexagons as hexagon_Hansen. The map of section 3.1.2 and the boxplots of section 3.1.3 are drawn from hexagon_Hansen.

TipThe ac() function

ac() is the function of the SpatialAcc package that computes the three measures of Part 1. The package is by Stamatis Kalogirou, the first author of the SAM paper (Kalogirou and Foley, 2006). The package manual titles ac() “Spatial Accessibility Measures”. According to the manual, the function “measures the accessibility of geographical areas to amenities”. Accessibility is defined in section 1 as “the measure of the capacity of a location to be reached from, or to be reached by, different locations”.

ac(p, n, D, d0, power = 2, family = "SAM")
Argument Meaning in the manual In this exercise
p the demand for services in each location the demand column of hexagons (section 2.3.3)
n the supply of services in each location the capacity column of eldercare (section 2.3.3)
D a matrix of a quantity separating the demand from the supply the road distance in kilometres, one row per hexagon and one column per centre (section 2.4)
d0 the threshold distance of the catchment 5 km, used by KD2SFCA; the value is also passed to SAM but is not used in the SAM formula
power the power of the separation variable 2, the value in the chapter’s code: the weight is \(e^{-2d}\) in Hansen, \(e^{-d^2}\) in KD2SFCA and \(1/d^2\) in SAM
family the accessibility measure "Hansen", "KD2SFCA" or "SAM"

ac() returns one value for each element of p, here one score for each hexagon. The table below shows how the capacity and the demand are used in the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures:

Measure Capacity of a centre (n) Demand of a hexagon (p)
Hansen (section 3.1) factor in the weight of the centre not used
KD2SFCA (section 3.2) numerator of the ratio \(R_j\) of the centre denominator of \(R_j\), summed over the hexagons in the catchment of the centre
SAM (section 3.3) numerator of the term of the centre, \(n_j / (p_i \, d_{ij}^{\beta})\) divisor of the score of the hexagon 
acc_Hansen <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                            eldercare$capacity,
                            distmat_km,
                            #d0 = 50,
                            power = 2,
                            family = "Hansen"))

colnames(acc_Hansen) <- "accHansen"
acc_Hansen <- as_tibble(acc_Hansen)
hexagon_Hansen <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_Hansen)
NoteHow the code works 
ac(p, n, D, d0, power, family)                            # SpatialAcc
bind_cols(...)                                            # dplyr
  • ac() takes the demand of each hexagon (p), the capacity of each centre (n), the distance matrix (D), a catchment distance (d0), a decay parameter (power) and the measure (family). It returns one number for each row of D, the accessibility of that hexagon.
  • data.frame() turns the vector into a one-column data frame, with a long column name made from the call. colnames() renames the column, and as_tibble() converts the data frame to a tibble.
  • bind_cols() adds the column to hexagons by position, so that the \(i\)-th value goes to the \(i\)-th hexagon. The result keeps the geometry of hexagons and is still an sf object.
  • d0 is commented out because the Hansen measure in ac() has no catchment.

Before bind_cols(), hexagons and acc_Hansen each have 3,125 rows. The first score is in bold:

hexagons:

fid demand geometry
1 100 POLYGON ((2667.5 27506.3, …))
2 100 POLYGON ((2667.5 25006.3, …))
… … …

acc_Hansen:

accHansen
1.6 × 10−14
1.1 × 10−16
…

After bind_cols(), hexagon_Hansen has the new column, which is shaded. The first score is in the row of hexagon 1:

fid demand accHansen geometry
1 100 1.6 × 10−14 POLYGON ((2667.5 27506.3, …))
2 100 1.1 × 10−16 POLYGON ((2667.5 25006.3, …))
… … … …

The chapter’s code then repeats the computation in a single code chunk, with power = 0.5. power = 2 and power = 0.5 give different scores (section 4.3).

TipThe Hansen formula in ac()

For each hexagon \(i\), ac(family = "Hansen") adds up the capacity of every centre \(j\), each multiplied by a weight that falls exponentially with distance (exponential decay, slide 8):

\[A_i = \sum_j n_j \, e^{-\beta d_{ij}} = \sum_j (\text{capacity of centre } j) \times (\text{distance weight of centre } j)\]

where the distance weight is \(e^{-\beta d}\), \(\beta\) is power and \(d\) is the road distance in kilometres. Every centre contributes to the sum, at any distance. The figure below shows invented centres along one road from a hexagon, at 0 m, 347 m, 1 km, 2 km and 3 km, and at the median road distance of all pairs of hexagon and centre in the data, 17.3 km.

With \(\beta = 2\), the weight is 1 for a centre at the hexagon and halves every 347 m. A centre 1 km away has a weight of 0.135. A centre at the median distance has a weight of about \(10^{-15}\).

The weight \(e^{-\beta d}\) falls faster with distance as \(\beta\) increases (chart below, as on slide 8). The chapter’s code uses \(\beta = 2\), drawn as the thick line.

TipLimits of the Hansen measure

No demand term. The formula contains the capacity \(n_j\) and the distance \(d_{ij}\). It has no demand term \(p_i\). Two hexagons at the same distances from the same centres get the same score, whether 10 or 10,000 residents aged 65 and over live in them. Luo and Wang (2003, equation 5) note this limitation of Hansen’s model: the model “considers only the ‘supply side’”. In the example below, two invented hexagons are 1 km from the same centre, which has a capacity of 100.

No unit. The score is a sum of weighted capacities, with no unit such as places per resident. A score of 42.5 cannot be interpreted on its own. Scores can only be compared with each other, for example to rank the hexagons. According to Long (2017, section 3), for such measures “there is no clear definition of what a high or low value should be, all analysis must be relative”.

tm_shape(shp, bbox)                                       # tmap
tm_polygons(fill, fill.scale, col_alpha)                  # tmap
tm_scale_intervals(style, n, values)                      # tmap

  • st_bbox() returns the bounding box of the hexagons: x from 2,668 to 50,010 m and y from 21,506 to 50,256 m in SVY21. Passed to tm_shape(bbox = mapex), the box fixes the extent of the map. Each map in Part 1 shows the hexagons, which have this extent already, so the maps have the same extent without bbox.
  • tm_polygons(fill = "accHansen") colours each hexagon by its score. tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10) divides the hexagons into ten classes of equal size (deciles), coloured from light to dark blue. col_alpha = 0.3, an addition to the chapter’s code, lightens the hexagon borders.

  • tm_compass(), tm_scalebar() and tm_grid() add a north arrow, a scale bar and a light coordinate grid.

In the invented example below, a layer has five hexagons. The maps in steps 3 and 4 show two of them. In steps 3 and 4, the other three hexagons are faded because they are left out of the map.

The classes are deciles: the 3,125 hexagons are sorted from the lowest score to the highest and divided into ten groups of 312 or 313 hexagons, about 10% of the hexagons each. The colour of a hexagon shows its decile. The table summarises the top decile, the middle 80% and the bottom decile:

Hexagons Hansen score Nearest centre by road Planning areas with the most hexagons
Top 10% 15.8 to 198 (median 30.8) 0.04 to 1.65 km (median 0.90) Bukit Merah, Ang Mo Kio, Tampines, Geylang
Middle 80% \(7.6 \times 10^{-11}\) to 15.8 (median 0.0683) 0.97 to 16.34 km (median 4.06) spread over all five regions

Of the 313 hexagons in the bottom decile, 73 have the same road distance to all 120 centres, an error in the distance matrix described in section 4.1.

The scores range over 26 orders of magnitude, because the weight \(e^{-2d}\) falls by a factor of 7.4 for each kilometre:

  • The highest score, 198, is at a hexagon in Bukit Merah. Its nearest centre is 0.37 km away by road, with a weight of 0.48. The hexagon has 16 centres within 2 km by road.
  • In the bottom decile, the median distance to the nearest centre is 17.71 km. A centre at that distance has a weight of about \(4.1 \times 10^{-16}\).
  • The highest score is more than \(10^{26}\) times the lowest score.
  • The lowest score is shared by hexagons 2930 and 2931 in Pasir Ris, each with the same road distance of 32.5 km to every centre, the error described in section 4.1.

areas_of <- function(g) {
  h_tab |>

}
named_areas <- mpsz |>

  st_cast("MULTIPOLYGON") |>

  mutate(area = st_area(geometry)) |>

3.2 Kernel density two-step floating catchment area (KD2SFCA)

TipFloating catchment area methods

KD2SFCA is the two-step floating catchment area method (2SFCA) with a distance weight inside the catchment. On slide 24, 2SFCA is described as “a special case of a potential model”. The table explains the three terms in the name 2SFCA:

Term Meaning
catchment the area within a threshold distance \(d_0\) of a point, here 5 km by road
floating a catchment of the same size, drawn around one point after another
two-step a catchment drawn twice: around every centre in step 1, then around every hexagon in step 2

In Luo and Wang (2003), the circle “floats from one centroid to another while its radius remains the same”. They trace 2SFCA to an earlier floating catchment area method with one step. That method draws a circle around each residential location. The accessibility of the location is the ratio of physicians to residents inside the circle, as if those physicians served only those residents. Luo and Wang (2003) call this assumption “obviously faulty”: a physician inside the circle also serves residents outside it.

Slides 25 and 26 show the two steps of 2SFCA, with physicians as the supply and residents as the demand. In this exercise, the supply is the capacity of a centre and the demand is the population of a hexagon:

  1. Step 1, from each centre. The ratio \(R_j\) is the capacity of centre \(j\) divided by the demand of all hexagons within \(d_0\) of the centre. \(R_j\) is the capacity per person in the catchment of the centre. When more people live in the catchment, \(R_j\) is smaller.
  2. Step 2, from each hexagon. The accessibility \(A_i\) of hexagon \(i\) is the sum of \(R_j\) over all centres within \(d_0\) of the hexagon.

The figure below shows the two steps with invented numbers and a catchment of 5 km. Hexagons and centres outside the circle are faded, because they are left out of the calculation.

In step 1, the 300 people within 5 km of centre A share its capacity of 3, so the ratio of centre A is 0.01. In step 2, the score of the hexagon is the sum of the ratios of centres A and B, each computed in step 1. Centre C is more than 5 km from the hexagon, so its ratio is left out of the sum. In step 1, the 5 km circle is drawn around each centre in turn, and in step 2 around each hexagon in turn.

The table compares the three measures:

Measure Catchment Demand of the hexagons Weight of a centre
Hansen (section 3.1) none: every centre is used not used \(e^{-\beta d}\), falls with distance
2SFCA \(d_0\) divides the capacity in step 1 1 inside the catchment, 0 outside
KD2SFCA \(d_0\) divides the capacity in step 1 falls with distance inside the catchment, 0 outside

Polzin et al. (2014) attribute KD2SFCA to Dai and Wang (2011). In KD2SFCA, the demand in step 1 and the ratios in step 2 are multiplied by the distance weight. A hexagon 500 m from a centre then has a larger weight in the demand of the centre than a hexagon 4.8 km away. The ratio of the centre also adds more to the score of the nearer hexagon.

In the example below, three invented hexagons share one centre with a capacity of 100. Hexagons 1 and 2 are 1 km from the centre. Hexagon 1 has 100 people. Hexagon 2 has 0 people in case X and 400 people in case Y. Hexagon 3, with 100 people, is 6 km from the centre, outside the 5 km catchment. The figure is not to scale.

Case X: hexagon 2 is empty. Case Y: 400 people live in hexagon 2.

Hexagon Hansen, power = 2 KD2SFCA, d0 = 5
case X case Y case X case Y
1 (1 km from A) 13.53 13.53 1 0.2
3 (6 km from A) 0.0006 0.0006 0 0
  • From case X to case Y, the Hansen score of hexagon 1 stays at 13.53.
  • From case X to case Y, the KD2SFCA score of hexagon 1 falls from 1 to 0.2, because in case Y the 500 people within the catchment share the capacity of 100.
  • Hexagon 3 is 6 km from the centre, outside the catchment, so its KD2SFCA score is 0 in case X and in case Y. Its Hansen score is small, but above 0.

3.2.1 KD2SFCA scores from ac()

The code in this section computes one KD2SFCA score for each of the 3,125 hexagons, with a catchment of 5 km, and adds the scores to the hexagons as hexagon_KD2SFCA. The map of section 3.2.2 and the boxplots of section 3.2.3 are drawn from hexagon_KD2SFCA.

acc_KD2SFCA <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                             eldercare$capacity,
                             distmat_km,
                             d0 = 5,
                             power = 2,
                             family = "KD2SFCA"))

colnames(acc_KD2SFCA) <- "accKD2SFCA"
acc_KD2SFCA <- as_tibble(acc_KD2SFCA)
hexagon_KD2SFCA <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_KD2SFCA)
NoteHow the code works
  • The call is the Hansen call of section 3.1.1 with family = "KD2SFCA" and a catchment of d0 = 5 km. In the chapter, the chunk is described as calculating “Hansen’s accessibility”, a description copied from section 17.6, which covers the Hansen measure.
TipThe 2SFCA formula and an example

Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 and 4) write the two steps as

\[R_j = \frac{S_j}{\sum_{k:\, d_{kj} \le d_0} P_k} = \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{\text{demand of the hexagons within } d_0 \text{ of centre } j}\]

\[A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} R_j = \text{sum of } R_j \text{ over the centres within } d_0 \text{ of hexagon } i\]

where \(S_j\) is the capacity of centre \(j\) and \(P_k\) is the demand of hexagon \(k\). In an invented example of four hexagons and two centres, centre A has a capacity of 1, centre B has a capacity of 3, and the catchment is 5 km:

km to A km to B demand centres within 5 km by hand ac(family = “2SFCA”)
hexagon 1 1 6 100 A 0.0025 0.0025
hexagon 2 2 4 200 A, B 0.0100 0.0100
hexagon 3 4 2 100 A, B 0.0100 0.0100
hexagon 4 6 1 100 B 0.0075 0.0075

The scores from ac() are the same as the hand calculation for all four hexagons.

Unit. The scores have a unit: capacity per person.

Average. Luo and Wang (2003) show that the average of the scores, weighted by demand, equals the total capacity divided by the total demand. In the example, \((100 \times 0.0025 + 200 \times 0.01 + 100 \times 0.01 + 100 \times 0.0075) / 500 = 0.008 = 4 / 500\). The same check is applied to the eldercare data in section 4.4.

TipThe KD2SFCA formula in ac()

In KD2SFCA, step 1 and step 2 of 2SFCA are each weighted by a kernel that falls with distance. According to the source of ac() (section 4.2), the kernel is \(e^{-d^{\beta}}\), where \(\beta\) is power:

\[R_j = \frac{n_j}{\sum_{k:\, d_{kj} \le d_0} p_k \, e^{-d_{kj}^{\beta}}}, \qquad A_i = \sum_{j:\, d_{ij} \le d_0} R_j \, e^{-d_{ij}^{\beta}}\]

With power = 2 and d0 = 5, a hexagon or centre inside the 5 km catchment has the weight \(e^{-d^2}\), with \(d\) in kilometres. A hexagon or centre outside the catchment has the weight 0. The figure below shows the weight at invented distances along one road from a hexagon.

The weight is 0.37 at 1 km and 0.018 at 2 km. At 5 km, the edge of the catchment, it is \(1.4 \times 10^{-11}\), and beyond 5 km it is 0.

The weight \(e^{-d^{\beta}}\) is \(e^{-1} = 0.37\) at 1 km for every \(\beta\). A larger \(\beta\) gives a larger weight below 1 km and a smaller weight above it, and every weight is 0 beyond 5 km (chart below; the dashed line is 2SFCA, with a weight of 1 inside the catchment).

TipLimits of the kernel in ac()

No width. The kernel \(e^{-d^2}\) has no parameter for its width, so its shape is the same for any catchment. The weight is below 0.02 beyond 2 km, so a centre beyond 2 km has less than 2% of the weight of a centre at the hexagon. The kernels of Dai and Wang (2011) and Cheng et al. (2016) are scaled by the catchment (section 4.4).

Unit of distance. The weight depends on the unit of the distances. A centre 2 km away has a weight of 0.018 with distances in kilometres, and a weight of 0 with distances in metres (section 4.2).

Hexagons KD2SFCA score Nearest centre by road Planning areas with the most hexagons

Of the 1,281 hexagons with a score of 0, 158 have the same road distance to every centre, an error in the distance matrix described in section 4.1.

The kernel \(e^{-d^2}\) is below 0.02 beyond 2 km:

  • The highest score, 1.48, is at a hexagon in Bukit Merah. The hexagon has 5 centres within 1 km by road.
  • Among the other scores above 0, the median distance to the nearest centre is 2.79 km. A centre at that distance has a weight of about \(4.2 \times 10^{-4}\).
  • A hexagon with no centre within 5 km by road scores 0, however many centres are just beyond 5 km.

3.3 Spatial accessibility measure (SAM)

TipSAM in Kalogirou and Foley (2006)

Kalogirou and Foley (2006) developed SAM to compare the accessibility of electoral divisions in Ireland to acute hospitals, for the existing hospitals and for the reforms proposed in the Hanly Report. The table lists their inputs and the inputs in this exercise:

Input Kalogirou and Foley (2006) This exercise
supply the number of beds of each hospital the capacity of each centre, 100
demand the population of each electoral division, and the population aged 65 and over the demand of each hexagon, 100
separation travel time by road road distance in kilometres

Section 4.5 replaces the demand of 100 with the residents aged 65 and over.

Kalogirou and Foley (2006) describe SAM as “a population-weighted accessibility score”. According to them, accessibility “increased the greater the local population and the number and/or size of facilities in the system” and “decreased the greater the distances from the place in question to those facilities”.

Each measure of Part 1 uses the demand in a different way:

Measure Demand used as a divisor Demand of other hexagons near the centre
Hansen none not used
2SFCA the demand of all hexagons within \(d_0\) of a centre, which divides the capacity of the centre more demand near the centre lowers the ratio \(R_j\) of the centre
SAM the demand of the hexagon itself, which divides the score of the hexagon not used

In the example below, two invented hexagons with 100 and 200 people are 1 km from the same centre, which has a capacity of 100.

Hexagon Hansen, power = 2 2SFCA, d0 = 5 SAM, power = 2
100 people 13.534 0.333 1.0
200 people 13.534 0.333 0.5

Under Hansen and under 2SFCA, the hexagons with 100 and 200 people have the same score. Under 2SFCA, the 300 people share the capacity of the centre, so each hexagon receives the same ratio. Under SAM, the hexagon with 200 people has half the score of the hexagon with 100 people.

3.3.1 SAM scores from ac()

The code in this section computes one SAM score for each of the 3,125 hexagons, and adds the scores to the hexagons as hexagon_SAM. The map of section 3.3.2 and the boxplots of section 3.3.3 are drawn from hexagon_SAM.

acc_SAM <- data.frame(ac(hexagons$demand,
                         eldercare$capacity,
                         distmat_km,
                         d0 = 5,
                         power = 2,
                         family = "SAM"))

colnames(acc_SAM) <- "accSAM"
acc_SAM <- as_tibble(acc_SAM)
hexagon_SAM <- bind_cols(hexagons, acc_SAM)
NoteHow the code works
  • The call is the KD2SFCA call with family = "SAM". In the chapter, this chunk is also described as calculating “Hansen’s accessibility”.
  • d0 = 5 has no effect on the SAM scores. The SAM formula of Kalogirou and Foley (2006) on slide 29 has no catchment. In the source of ac() (section 4.2), d0 is used only for 2SFCA and KD2SFCA. The argument is carried over from the KD2SFCA call: with d0 = 50 in place of d0 = 5, every SAM score was the same.
TipThe SAM formula in ac()

Slide 29 shows the formula of Kalogirou and Foley (2006). According to the source of ac() (section 4.2), the function computes SAM as

\[A_i = \sum_j \frac{n_j}{p_i \, d_{ij}^{\,\beta}} = \frac{1}{\text{demand of hexagon } i} \sum_j \frac{\text{capacity of centre } j}{(\text{road distance from hexagon } i \text{ to centre } j)^{\beta}}\]

where \(\beta\) is power. The weight of a centre is the power function \(1/d^{\beta}\) of slide 8. Stewart’s model on slide 19 and Hansen (1959) use the same function. The figure below shows the weight with power = 2, at invented distances along one road from a hexagon.

The weight is divided by 4 each time the distance doubles. At the median distance of 17.3 km it is 0.0033, about \(3.6 \times 10^{12}\) times the weight of about \(10^{-15}\) in the Hansen formula of ac() (section 3.1.1).

The weight \(1/d^{\beta}\) is 1 at 1 km for every \(\beta\). A larger \(\beta\) gives a larger weight below 1 km and a smaller weight above it (chart below, as on slide 8). The vertical axis is cut at 4, although the weight grows without limit as the distance approaches zero.

The table below gives the SAM and 2SFCA scores of the example of section 3.2.1, with power = 2:

km to A km to B demand Σ n_j / d² SAM by hand ac(family = “SAM”) 2SFCA
hexagon 1 1 6 100 1.0833 0.0108 0.0108 0.0025
hexagon 2 2 4 200 0.4375 0.0022 0.0022 0.0100
hexagon 3 4 2 100 0.8125 0.0081 0.0081 0.0100
hexagon 4 6 1 100 3.0278 0.0303 0.0303 0.0075

The scores from ac() are the same as the hand calculation. Hexagon 4, 1 km from the larger centre B, has the highest SAM score. Hexagon 2 has the lowest SAM score, because its demand of 200 is twice the demand of the other hexagons. In 2SFCA, hexagons 2 and 3 have the same score, the highest of the four hexagons, because each is within 5 km of centres A and B.

TipLimits of SAM in ac()

No upper limit near a centre. The power function grows without limit as the distance approaches zero. The shortest distance in the matrix is 37 m. At that distance, the weight is 733, the weight of 733 centres at 1 km.

No catchment. The SAM formula has no catchment, so the score of every hexagon includes every centre, at any distance.

Demand used once. In ac(), the demand enters the score once (section 4.2), whereas the formula on slide 29 uses it twice.

Division by zero. A hexagon with a demand of 0 has an infinite score (section 4.5).

3.4 Summary of Part 1

In every panel, hexagon \(i\) has 100 people and hexagon \(k\) has 300, and centres A and B each have a capacity of 100. The roads are 1, 2, 4 and 8 km long, and their lengths in the drawing are schematic. Hexagons, centres and roads that a measure does not use are faded.

When the number of people in hexagon \(i\) increases, the Hansen score of \(i\) stays at 106.25. The SAM and 2SFCA scores of \(i\) fall (left). When the number of people in hexagon \(k\) increases, the Hansen and SAM scores of \(i\) stay the same. The 2SFCA score of \(i\) falls towards 1, the ratio of centre B, because centre B is 8 km from \(k\) and only the 100 people of \(i\) are within its 5 km catchment (right). The dots mark the example in the five-panel figure above, with 100 people in \(i\) and 300 people in \(k\).

Measure Unit of the score The input it adds
1. Nearest centre kilometres nothing: only the closest centre counts
2. Hansen none the capacity of every centre
3. 2SFCA capacity per person the people within 5 km of a centre, who share its capacity
4. KD2SFCA capacity per person a weight that falls with distance inside the 5 km catchment
SAM (side branch) none the people of the hexagon itself, as the divisor of its score

The 300 people of hexagon \(k\) lower the capacity per person of centre A in panels 3 and 4. The weights in panel 4 are \(1 - (d/5)^2\), the kernel of Dai and Wang (2011) without its factor 3/4. The factor cancels between step 1 and step 2. The weight in ac() is \(e^{-d^2}\), which has no parameter that sets how fast the weight falls (section 3.2). Panels 2 and 5 use the power function \(1/d^2\) of Hansen (1959). With ac(family = "Hansen"), which uses \(e^{-2d}\) (section 3.1.1), hexagon \(i\) scores \(100 e^{-2} + 100 e^{-8} =\) 13.57, against 106.25 in panel 2.

4.1 Network distances: missing routes and the straight-line lower bound

In the network analysis of Kalogirou and Foley (2006, p. 55), no distance was found for some electoral divisions, “primarily on islands”. The 9,090 residents of those divisions, 0.23% of the resident population of Ireland in the 2002 census, were left out of their model. In chapter 17, distmat_km is used without a check for missing distances. A network distance follows the roads (Long, 2017, section 2.2; slide 6), so it is at least as long as the straight line between the same two points. Comparing each network distance with the straight-line distance of the same pair is an extension of the course material, based on that definition.

The question for this section is whether the distances in OD_Matrix.csv satisfy two conditions: no network distance is shorter than the straight line, and the distances from a hexagon to different centres differ.

hex_xy <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(st_geometry(hexagons)))
ctr_xy <- st_coordinates(eldercare)
euclid_km <- sqrt(outer(hex_xy[, 1], ctr_xy[, 1], "-")^2 +
                  outer(hex_xy[, 2], ctr_xy[, 2], "-")^2) / 1000
detour <- distmat_km / euclid_km

c(pairs = length(detour),
  median_ratio = median(detour),
  network_shorter = sum(detour < 1))
          pairs    median_ratio network_shorter 
   3.750000e+05    1.324201e+00    9.512000e+03
NoteHow the code works 
st_centroid(x); st_coordinates(x)                         # sf
outer(X, Y, FUN = "-")                                    # base R
  • st_centroid() returns the centre of each hexagon, and st_coordinates() returns the x and y of each centre in metres.
  • outer(X, Y, "-") subtracts every coordinate of a centre from every coordinate of a hexagon, and returns a matrix of 3,125 hexagons by 120 centres. The straight-line distance is the square root of the sum of the squared x and y differences, divided by 1000 to give kilometres.
  • detour divides each network distance by the straight-line distance of the same pair.

The median network distance is 1.32 times the straight-line distance. The first condition fails for 9,512 of the 375,000 pairs of hexagon and centre: their network distance is shorter than the straight line.

od_check <- ODMatrix |>
  group_by(origin_id) |>
  summarise(distinct_costs = n_distinct(total_cost))

broken_fid <- od_check$origin_id[od_check$distinct_costs == 1]
length(broken_fid)
[1] 159
NoteHow the code works 
n_distinct(x)                                             # dplyr
  • For each hexagon, n_distinct() counts the different values of total_cost among its 120 rows. A hexagon with a different distance to each of the 120 centres has 120 distinct values of total_cost.

Of the 3,125 hexagons, 159 have one value of total_cost for all 120 centres.

centre_exit <- ODMatrix |>
  filter(!origin_id %in% broken_fid) |>
  distinct(destination_id, exit_cost)

ODMatrix |>
  filter(origin_id %in% broken_fid) |>
  distinct(origin_id, exit_cost) |>
  left_join(centre_exit, by = "exit_cost") |>
  count(destination_id)
# A tibble: 1 × 2
  destination_id     n
           <dbl> <int>
1            133   159
NoteHow the code works
  • exit_cost is the distance from the road to a centre, so each centre has one value, the same for every hexagon. centre_exit lists that value for each centre, from the hexagons with valid rows.
  • The join matches the exit_cost of each of the 159 hexagons to the centre with that value, and count() counts the hexagons per centre.

All 159 hexagons carry the exit cost of centre 133, the last centre in the file. Their rows hold the distance to centre 133, repeated for every other centre. The pattern is consistent with a network analysis in which no route was found from these hexagons, and their rows were filled with the result for the last centre.

Of the 159 hexagons, 87 are in the Western Water Catchment and 18 in the Southern Islands. The other 54 are scattered along the coast and the edges of the reservoirs. Of the 159, 94 have a centre within 5 km in a straight line, so their KD2SFCA score of 0 in section 3.2 may be wrong. One hexagon, 1067, near International Business Park, has a repeated distance of 4.97 km, so all 120 centres are inside its catchment of 5 km.

In the rest of Part 2, the 159 hexagons are left out of every calculation and mapped in grey. The accessibility measures are computed on the other 2,966 hexagons and their rows of the distance matrix:

D <- distmat_km[ok, ]
p100 <- hexagons$demand[ok]
n100 <- eldercare$capacity
