4.2 Formulas in ac(): code versus slides and readings

In section 3, ac() was called three times, for the Hansen, KD2SFCA and SAM measures. No formula for the three measures is given in chapter 17. The authors of the readings write out the formula of each measure they compute: Hansen (1959, p. 5), Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 to 6), Luo and Qi (2009, equations 1 to 5), Polzin et al. (2014, equations 3 and 4), Cheng et al. (2016, equations 1 to 5) and Kalogirou and Foley (2006, p. 58). On the slides, formulas are given for Stewart’s potential model (slide 19), 2SFCA (slides 25 and 26), E2SFCA (slide 27) and SAM (slide 29). Slide 8 shows the two usual forms of distance decay: the power function \(\alpha / d^{\beta}\) and the exponential function \(\alpha e^{-\beta d}\). The source of ac(), about 50 lines long, is printed by typing the name of the function:

SpatialAcc::ac
function (p, n, D, d0, power = 2, family = "SAM") 
{
    family <- match.arg(family, c("SAM", "2SFCA", "KD2SFCA", 
        "Hansen", "log"))
    D <- as.matrix(D)
    if (length(p) != nrow(D)) {
        stop("length of 'p' must equal nrow(D)")
    }
    if (length(n) != ncol(D)) {
        stop("length of 'n' must equal ncol(D)")
    }
    if (family %in% c("2SFCA", "KD2SFCA") && missing(d0)) {
        stop("'d0' is required for family '2SFCA' and 'KD2SFCA'")
    }
    if (family == "SAM") {
        ac.matrix <- t(n/t(p * (D^power)))
        ac.measure <- rowSums(ac.matrix)
    }
    else if (family == "2SFCA") {
        D[D > d0] <- 0
        D[D > 0] <- 1
        step1 <- p * D
        Rj <- n/colSums(step1)
        step2 <- t(Rj * t(D))
        step2[is.nan(step2)] <- 0
        ac.measure <- rowSums(step2)
    }
    else if (family == "KD2SFCA") {
        D[D > d0] <- 0
        D0 <- D
        D0[D > 0] <- 1
        step1 <- p * exp(-D^power)
        step1 <- step1 * D0
        Rj <- n/colSums(step1)
        step2 <- t(Rj * t(exp(-D^power)))
        step2 <- step2 * D0
        step2[is.nan(step2)] <- 0
        ac.measure <- rowSums(step2)
    }
    else if (family == "Hansen") {
        ac.matrix <- n * exp(-power * D)
        ac.measure <- rowSums(ac.matrix)
    }
    else {
        ac.matrix <- log(n * exp(-power * D))/power
        ac.measure <- rowSums(ac.matrix)
    }
    return(ac.measure)
}
<bytecode: 0xc630029a8>
<environment: namespace:SpatialAcc>

The table lists each value of the family argument of ac() beside its definition in the slides and the readings.

Family Computed by ac() In the slides or the readings Difference
Hansen \(\sum_j n_j e^{-\beta d_{ij}}\) Hansen (1959, p. 5): \(\sum_j S_j / T_{ij}^{x}\); slide 19 (Stewart): \(\sum_j M_j / d_{ij}^{\alpha}\) exponential decay in ac(), power function in Hansen’s thesis
2SFCA \(\sum_{j: d_{ij} \le d_0} n_j / \sum_{k: d_{kj} \le d_0} p_k\) slides 25 and 26; Luo and Wang (2003, equations 3 and 4) none
KD2SFCA 2SFCA with each term multiplied by \(e^{-d^{\beta}}\) Dai and Wang (2011), according to Polzin et al. (2014, equation 4): \(\tfrac{3}{4}(1 - (d/d_0)^2)\); Cheng et al. (2016, equation 3): \(e^{-d^2/k}\) the kernel of ac() has no width parameter, so its shape is the same for every \(d_0\)
SAM \(\sum_j n_j / (p_i \, d_{ij}^{\beta})\) slide 29: \(\frac{1}{p_i} \sum_j n_j / (p_i \, d_{ij}^2)\) \(p_i\) appears once in ac() and twice on the slide; d0 is not used

Hansen’s thesis says that “an exponential function of distance should be used”, and then explains that “the measurement of distance separating the various areas should be raised to some power”. In the thesis, the “exponential function of distance” is the distance raised to a power. ac() computes the exponential function of slide 8, e raised to a multiple of the distance.

The chart shows the weight of each kernel on this page at each distance, together with the distribution of the distance from each hexagon to its nearest centre.

  • Chart
  • Code
k_cheng <- 5^2 / log(20)
near <- apply(D, 1, min)
near_med <- median(near)

kernels <- list(
  `Hansen, power = 2: exp(-2d)`         = \(d) exp(-2 * d),
  `Hansen, power = 0.5: exp(-0.5d)`     = \(d) exp(-0.5 * d),
  `power function: 1/d²`                = \(d) pmin(1, 1 / d^2),
  `KD2SFCA in ac(): exp(-d²)`           = \(d) exp(-d^2) * (d <= 5),
  `Epanechnikov, d0 = 5 km`             = \(d) (1 - (d / 5)^2) * (d <= 5),
  `Gaussian of Cheng et al., d0 = 5 km` = \(d) exp(-d^2 / k_cheng) * (d <= 5),
  `2SFCA, d0 = 5 km`                    = \(d) as.numeric(d <= 5))
k_col <- c("#08519c", "#6baed6", "#31a354", "#e6550d", "#fdae6b", "#756bb1", "#666666")
k_thick <- c(TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)  # the chapter's two kernels

d <- sort(c(seq(0, 10, by = 0.05), near_med))
p_decay <- plotly::plot_ly()
for (k in seq_along(kernels)) {
  name <- names(kernels)[k]
  p_decay <- p_decay |>
    plotly::add_lines(x = d, y = kernels[[k]](d), name = name, legendgroup = name,
                      line = list(color = k_col[k], width = if (k_thick[k]) 4 else 2,
                                  dash = if (k == 7) "dash" else "solid"),
                      hovertemplate = "%{y:.3g}") |>
    plotly::add_markers(x = near_med, y = kernels[[k]](near_med), name = name,
                        legendgroup = name, showlegend = FALSE,
                        marker = list(color = k_col[k], size = 10), hoverinfo = "skip")
}
median_line <- list(dash = "dot", color = "#4d4d4d", width = 1.5)
median_hover <- sprintf("median distance to the nearest centre: %.2f km", near_med)
p_decay <- p_decay |>
  plotly::add_lines(x = c(near_med, near_med), y = c(0, 1), line = median_line,
                    name = "median", showlegend = FALSE, hovertemplate = median_hover) |>
  plotly::layout(yaxis = list(title = "weight"))

bins <- tibble(d = near) |>
  count(lo = floor(d / 0.25) * 0.25) |>
  mutate(range = sprintf("%.2f to %.2f km", lo, lo + 0.25))
p_near <- plotly::plot_ly(bins, x = ~lo + 0.125, y = ~n, type = "bar", customdata = ~range,
                          name = "nearest centre", showlegend = FALSE,
                          marker = list(color = "#999999"),
                          hovertemplate = "%{customdata}, %{y} hexagons") |>
  plotly::add_lines(x = c(near_med, near_med), y = c(0, max(bins$n)), line = median_line,
                    name = "median", showlegend = FALSE, hovertemplate = median_hover,
                    inherit = FALSE) |>
  plotly::layout(yaxis = list(title = "hexagons"), bargap = 0.05)

plotly::subplot(p_decay, p_near, nrows = 2, shareX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE,
                heights = c(0.65, 0.35), margin = 0.04) |>
  plotly::layout(
    hovermode = "x unified",
    xaxis = list(title = "network distance d (km)", range = c(0, 10), hoverformat = ".2f"),
    legend = list(orientation = "h", x = 0, y = 1.02, yanchor = "bottom"),
    margin = list(t = 120),
    annotations = list(list(xref = "x", yref = "y2", x = near_med, y = max(bins$n),
                            xanchor = "left", yanchor = "top", showarrow = FALSE,
                            bgcolor = "rgba(255, 255, 255, 0.85)",
                            text = sprintf(paste0("  median distance from a hexagon<br>",
                                                  "  to its nearest centre: %.1f km"), near_med))))
NoteHow the code works 
plot_ly(); add_lines(x, y, name, line, hovertemplate)     # plotly
add_markers(x, y, marker); count(x, ...)                  # plotly, dplyr
subplot(..., nrows, shareX, heights); layout(...)         # plotly
  • k_cheng is the width of the Gaussian kernel of Cheng et al. (2016), chosen so that the weight at the edge of the catchment is 0.05: \(e^{-25/k} = 0.05\) gives \(k = 25 / \ln 20 = 8.35 \text{ km}^2\).
  • near is the distance from each of the 2,966 hexagons to its nearest centre.
  • near_med is the median of near.
  • Each element of kernels is one kernel, written as a function of the distance \(d\). The Epanechnikov kernel is drawn without its factor 3/4. The power function is capped at 1. With these two changes, every kernel has the value 1 at a distance of 0. The factor 3/4 and the cap apply to the chart only. In section 4.3, the power function is computed without a cap. In KD2SFCA, the factor 3/4 cancels between step 1 and step 2.
  • add_lines() draws each kernel from 0 to 10 km, twice the catchment of 5 km. The median distance is added to the distances, so that the hover text shows the weight at the median.
  • add_markers() adds a dot on each kernel at the median distance.
  • The kernels of the chapter’s code, Hansen with power = 2 and KD2SFCA in ac(), are drawn thick. 2SFCA is dashed.
  • count() counts the hexagons in bins of 0.25 km.
  • plot_ly(type = "bar") draws the counts.
  • A second add_lines() in each panel draws the dotted line at the median distance.
  • subplot(shareX = TRUE) places the histogram under the kernels, on one distance axis.
  • hovermode = "x unified" shows the weight of every kernel at the distance under the mouse.

The median distance from a hexagon to its nearest centre is 3.8 km. At 3.8 km, the KD2SFCA kernel of ac() is \(5.1 \times 10^{-7}\), and the Hansen weight with power = 2 is \(4.9 \times 10^{-4}\). At the same distance, the Epanechnikov kernel of the readings is 0.42, and the Gaussian kernel of Cheng et al. is 0.18. The kernel of ac() is 0.018 at 2 km, so the centres between 2 and 5 km away have weights below 0.018.

The kernel of ac() is applied to the distances in the unit of the matrix, with no conversion. A centre 2 km away has a weight of 0.018 with distances in kilometres and a weight of 0 with distances in metres. The kernel of Cheng et al. (2016) divides the squared distance by a width \(k\) set from the size of the catchment, so its weights are the same in kilometres and in metres.

4.3 Hansen model: exponential versus power decay, and unequal capacities

In section 3.1, Hansen’s measure was computed with power = 2. In the chapter’s single code chunk, the calculation is repeated with power = 0.5. The scores for power = 2 and power = 0.5 are not compared. Luo and Wang (2003, Table 1) computed their gravity measure with seven values of \(\beta\), from 1.0 to 2.2, and found a larger variance of the scores with a larger \(\beta\). Hansen (1959) measured one exponent for each trip purpose: 2.20 for work trips, 2.35 for social trips and 3.00 for shopping trips, with travel time in minutes (p. 9). He considered the relative measures of accessibility “not particularly sensitive to small variations in the exponent of distance” (p. 35). On slide 19, the exponent of distance in Stewart’s model, written \(\alpha\), is “usually between 1 and 2”. In ac(), power is the \(\beta\) of an exponential function, whereas Hansen (1959) used a power function of distance (section 4.2).

In all six readings that compute a measure, the supply differs between locations: the jobs, retail sales or population of each zone in Hansen (1959), the physicians at each location in Luo and Wang (2003) and Luo and Qi (2009), the physicians of each hospital in Polzin et al. (2014), the practising doctors of each hospital in Cheng et al. (2016) and the beds of each hospital in Kalogirou and Foley (2006). In chapter 17, every centre has a capacity of 100, so ac() is not run with unequal capacities. Testing ac() with unequal capacities is an extension of the course material, based on the source of ac() printed in section 4.2.

The question for this section is how much the choice of decay changes the ranking of the hexagons, and whether ac() weights each centre by its own capacity.

hansen <- tibble(
  `exp(-2d)` = ac(p100, n100, D, power = 2, family = "Hansen"),
  `exp(-0.5d)` = ac(p100, n100, D, power = 0.5, family = "Hansen"),
  `1/d²` = as.vector(D^-2 %*% n100))

cor(hansen, method = "spearman") |>
  kable(digits = 3)
exp(-2d) exp(-0.5d) 1/d²
exp(-2d) 1.00 0.950 0.960
exp(-0.5d) 0.95 1.000 0.989
1/d² 0.96 0.989 1.000
NoteHow the code works
  • The first two columns are the chapter’s two calls. The third column is the power function of slide 19 with \(\alpha = 2\): D^-2 raises every distance to the power -2, and the matrix product %*% with the capacities sums \(n_j / d_{ij}^2\) over the centres for each hexagon.
  • cor(method = "spearman") correlates the ranks of the hexagons under each pair of measures.

The ranks are similar under the three measures, with rank correlations of 0.95 to 0.99. The spread of the scores differs: the highest score is 1,916 times the median with power = 2, 12 times with power = 0.5, and 815 times with \(1/d^2\). With power = 2, a centre 700 m away has a quarter of the weight of a centre next to the hexagon, since \(e^{-1.4} = 0.25\). With power = 2, a map with ten equal intervals would place 91% of the hexagons in the lowest class.

With a demand of 100 in every hexagon and power = 2, the SAM scores of the 2,966 hexagons equal the 1/d² column divided by 100. The hexagons therefore have the same rank order under SAM and under the Hansen measure with \(1/d^2\).

hex_ok <- filter(hexagons, od_ok)

decile_map <- function(data, var, title, palette = "brewer.blues") {
  tm_shape(hexagons, bbox = mapex) +
    tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col_alpha = 0) +
  tm_shape(data) +
    tm_polygons(fill = var,
                fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "quantile", n = 10,
                                                values = palette),
                fill.legend = tm_legend(show = FALSE),
                col_alpha = 0) +
    tm_title(title, size = 0.9) +
    tm_layout(frame = FALSE)
}

tmap_arrange(
  decile_map(bind_cols(hex_ok, hansen), "exp(-2d)", "Hansen, exp(-2d)"),
  decile_map(bind_cols(hex_ok, hansen), "exp(-0.5d)", "Hansen, exp(-0.5d)"),
  decile_map(bind_cols(hex_ok, hansen), "1/d²", "Power function, 1/d²"),
  ncol = 3)
NoteHow the code works
  • decile_map() draws all hexagons in grey, then the valid hexagons coloured by deciles of one score, with no legend, so that several maps can be compared by pattern. The 159 hexagons of section 4.1 stay grey.
  • tmap_arrange() places the three maps in one row.

Drawn in deciles, the three maps are close to identical, as the rank correlations indicate. The choice of decay changes the size of the differences between hexagons, and the deciles keep only their order.

The capacity argument n of ac() has one value per centre. In the source printed in section 4.2, the Hansen family computes n * exp(-power * D). D is a matrix with one row per hexagon, and n has one value per centre. R multiplies a matrix by a vector element by element, down the columns, starting the vector again from its first value when the vector is shorter than the matrix. The first value of n is therefore applied to the weight of the first hexagon for centre 1, the second value to the weight of the second hexagon for centre 1, and each later value to the weight of the next hexagon. The capacity of centre \(j\) should multiply every weight for centre \(j\).

The example of section 3.2.1 has four hexagons and two centres, with a capacity of 1 for centre A and 3 for centre B:

tibble(hexagon = 1:4,
       `ac(family = "Hansen")` = ac(toy_p, toy_n, toy_D, power = 0.5,
                                    family = "Hansen"),
       `by hand` = as.vector(exp(-0.5 * toy_D) %*% toy_n)) |>
  kable(digits = 3)
hexagon ac(family = “Hansen”) by hand
1 0.656 0.756
2 1.510 0.774
3 0.503 1.239
4 1.969 1.869
NoteHow the code works
  • exp(-0.5 * toy_D) %*% toy_n is the matrix product: for each hexagon, the sum over the centres of the weight times the capacity of that centre.

Hexagons 2 and 3 have swapped distances: each is 2 km from one centre and 4 km from the other. Hexagon 3 is 2 km from the larger centre B and should score higher, as it does by hand (1.24 against 0.77). ac() gives the opposite order (0.5 against 1.51). The chapter’s scores are correct, because every centre has a capacity of 100. With actual capacities, the Hansen family of ac() gives wrong scores. The matrix product above is the correct calculation. The 2SFCA and KD2SFCA families of ac() divide by colSums() and transpose the weight matrix before multiplying it by the capacities. For the toy example of section 3.2.1, with the same unequal capacities, 2SFCA gives the same result by hand and with ac().

4.4 Floating catchment methods: kernel shape and catchment size

In section 3.2, KD2SFCA was computed once, with the kernel of ac() and a catchment of 5 km. The kernel gives weights below 0.018 beyond 2 km (section 4.2). In 2SFCA (slides 24 to 26), every centre within the catchment counts equally. In E2SFCA (slides 27 and 28), the catchment is divided into three zones with decreasing weights. In KD2SFCA (Polzin et al., 2014), a continuous kernel replaces the zones.

Luo and Wang (2003) computed 2SFCA with seven catchments, from 20 to 50 minutes, and found that the scores had a lower variance with a larger catchment. Luo and Qi (2009) computed E2SFCA with two sets of zone weights. On p. 1104, they report that 2SFCA gives higher scores than E2SFCA in areas of poor access, which they attribute to the assumption of equal access inside the catchment in 2SFCA. They also find that 2SFCA identifies a smaller total shortage area than E2SFCA. With the weights of set 2, which decrease faster with distance, E2SFCA identifies a larger total shortage area than with the weights of set 1 (Luo and Qi, 2009, p. 1104; speaker notes of slide 28). Polzin et al. (2014) compared the Epanechnikov kernel of Dai and Wang (2011) with a quartic kernel. Cheng et al. (2016) set the width of a Gaussian kernel so that the weight at the edge of the catchment is 0.05.

Luo and Wang (2003) show that, in 2SFCA, the average accessibility weighted by demand equals the total supply divided by the total demand, provided every centre has some demand within its catchment. The capacity of each centre is allocated to the hexagons in its catchment. In E2SFCA and KD2SFCA, the same weights enter step 1 and step 2, so the capacity is allocated in the same way, and the same equality holds.

The question for this section is how much the scores depend on the kernel and on the size of the catchment, and whether each computation satisfies the property of Luo and Wang (2003).

fca_weights <- function(D, kernel, d0 = 5) {
  W <- switch(kernel,
    step = (D <= d0) * 1,
    ac_default = exp(-D^2) * (D <= d0),
    epanechnikov = (1 - (D / d0)^2) * (D <= d0),
    cheng = exp(-D^2 / (d0^2 / log(20))) * (D <= d0),
    e2sfca_1 = c(1, 0.68, 0.22, 0)[findInterval(D, c(d0 / 3, 2 * d0 / 3, d0),
                                                left.open = TRUE) + 1],
    e2sfca_2 = c(1, 0.42, 0.09, 0)[findInterval(D, c(d0 / 3, 2 * d0 / 3, d0),
                                                left.open = TRUE) + 1])
  matrix(W, nrow = nrow(D))
}

fca <- function(p, n, D, kernel, d0 = 5) {
  W <- fca_weights(D, kernel, d0)
  R <- n / colSums(p * W)
  R[!is.finite(R)] <- 0
  as.vector(W %*% R)
}
NoteHow the code works
  • fca_weights() returns a matrix of the same shape as D, with the weight of each pair under one kernel. (D <= d0) is TRUE inside the catchment and FALSE outside, which become 1 and 0 when multiplied. For E2SFCA, findInterval() returns 0, 1, 2 or 3 for a distance in the first, second or third zone or beyond the catchment. The weight is then looked up in a vector of four zone weights. The zones are thirds of the catchment, in place of the 10-minute zones of a 30-minute catchment on slide 27. The zone weights of e2sfca_1 and e2sfca_2 are weight sets 1 and 2 of Luo and Qi (2009).
  • fca() computes the two steps of section 3.2.1 with any kernel. colSums(p * W) is the weighted demand in the catchment of each centre (p * W multiplies row \(i\) of W by the demand of hexagon \(i\)), and R is the ratio of capacity to weighted demand for each centre. For a centre with no demand in its catchment, the ratio is capacity divided by 0, and is set to 0, as in ac(). The matrix product W %*% R is step 2, the weighted sum of the ratios for each hexagon.
fca_scores <- tibble(
  `2SFCA` = fca(p100, n100, D, "step"),
  `E2SFCA, weights 1` = fca(p100, n100, D, "e2sfca_1"),
  `E2SFCA, weights 2` = fca(p100, n100, D, "e2sfca_2"),
  `KD2SFCA, ac() kernel` = fca(p100, n100, D, "ac_default"),
  `KD2SFCA, Epanechnikov` = fca(p100, n100, D, "epanechnikov"),
  `KD2SFCA, Cheng et al.` = fca(p100, n100, D, "cheng"))

c(same_as_ac_2SFCA = all.equal(fca_scores$`2SFCA`,
                               ac(p100, n100, D, d0 = 5, family = "2SFCA")),
  same_as_ac_KD2SFCA = all.equal(fca_scores$`KD2SFCA, ac() kernel`,
                                 ac(p100, n100, D, d0 = 5, power = 2,
                                    family = "KD2SFCA")))
  same_as_ac_2SFCA same_as_ac_KD2SFCA 
              TRUE               TRUE

fca() reproduces the scores of ac() for 2SFCA and KD2SFCA. The table lists, for each method, the weighted mean of the property of Luo and Wang (2003), with three other summaries:

fca_scores |>
  summarise(across(everything(),
                   list(weighted_mean = \(a) weighted.mean(a, p100),
                        sd = sd,
                        zeros = \(a) sum(a == 0),
                        max = max))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(),
               names_to = c("method", ".value"),
               names_pattern = "(.*)_(weighted_mean|sd|zeros|max)") |>
  kable(digits = 4)
method weighted_mean sd zeros max
2SFCA 0.0405 0.0502 1123 0.2274
E2SFCA, weights 1 0.0405 0.0565 1123 0.3476
E2SFCA, weights 2 0.0405 0.0619 1123 0.4816
KD2SFCA, ac() kernel 0.0405 0.1240 1123 1.4756
KD2SFCA, Epanechnikov 0.0405 0.0566 1123 0.3178
KD2SFCA, Cheng et al. 0.0405 0.0602 1123 0.4040
NoteHow the code works
  • summarise(across()) computes four statistics for every column: the mean weighted by demand, the standard deviation, the number of hexagons with a score of 0, and the maximum. pivot_longer() with names_pattern splits each column name into the method and the statistic, so that each method is one row.

The total capacity is 120 × 100 = 12,000 and the total demand is 2,966 × 100, so the ratio is 0.0405. Every method has a weighted mean equal to that ratio, the property of Luo and Wang (2003), which is consistent with every centre having some demand within 5 km. Every method has the same 1,123 hexagons at zero, since every method uses the catchment of 5 km. The scores from the kernel of ac() have more than twice the standard deviation of the scores from the Epanechnikov and Gaussian kernels. The weights of the ac() kernel fall to 0.37 at 1 km and 0.018 at 2 km, so its scores are concentrated on hexagons near a centre.

When the 2SFCA scores are computed on all 3,125 hexagons, including the 159 hexagons of section 4.1, the highest score, 0.93, is at hexagon 1067, which has all 120 centres at a repeated distance of 4.97 km.

fca_scores |>
  filter(`2SFCA` > 0) |>
  cor(method = "spearman") |>
  kable(digits = 2)
2SFCA E2SFCA, weights 1 E2SFCA, weights 2 KD2SFCA, ac() kernel KD2SFCA, Epanechnikov KD2SFCA, Cheng et al.
2SFCA 1.00 0.93 0.88 0.67 0.92 0.89
E2SFCA, weights 1 0.93 1.00 0.99 0.86 0.99 0.99
E2SFCA, weights 2 0.88 0.99 1.00 0.91 0.97 0.99
KD2SFCA, ac() kernel 0.67 0.86 0.91 1.00 0.86 0.90
KD2SFCA, Epanechnikov 0.92 0.99 0.97 0.86 1.00 0.99
KD2SFCA, Cheng et al. 0.89 0.99 0.99 0.90 0.99 1.00
NoteHow the code works
  • The 1,123 hexagons with a score of 0 under every method are left out. Tied at the bottom of every ranking, they would raise all the correlations.

Among the hexagons with a centre within 5 km, the rank correlations among 2SFCA, E2SFCA and the Epanechnikov and Gaussian kernels of KD2SFCA range from 0.88 to 0.99. The scores from the kernel of ac() have their lowest rank correlation with the 2SFCA scores, 0.67.

fca_sf <- bind_cols(hex_ok, fca_scores)
tmap_arrange(
  decile_map(fca_sf, "2SFCA", "2SFCA, 5 km"),
  decile_map(fca_sf, "E2SFCA, weights 2", "E2SFCA, weights 2"),
  decile_map(fca_sf, "KD2SFCA, ac() kernel", "KD2SFCA, kernel of ac()"),
  decile_map(fca_sf, "KD2SFCA, Cheng et al.", "KD2SFCA, Gaussian of Cheng et al."),
  ncol = 2)

Under 2SFCA, the scores change in steps, at the distances where a centre enters or leaves the catchment of a hexagon. E2SFCA has three smaller steps per centre. The scores under the Gaussian kernel of Cheng et al. (2016) decline smoothly from each centre. The scores from the kernel of ac() are highest within 1 km of a centre, where the weight is at least 0.37, and the weight is below 0.018 at more than 2 km from a centre.

Luo and Wang (2003) tested catchments of 20 to 50 minutes for physicians. Users of eldercare may travel less far than patients of a physician, and a smaller catchment is then plausible. The table lists the results for catchments of 2 to 15 km:

map_dfr(c(2, 3, 5, 8, 10, 15), \(d0) {
  a <- fca(p100, n100, D, "step", d0)
  tibble(d0_km = d0,
         sd = sd(a),
         hexagons_at_zero = sum(a == 0),
         centres_without_demand = sum(colSums(D <= d0) == 0),
         weighted_mean = weighted.mean(a, p100))
}) |>
  kable(digits = 4)
d0_km sd hexagons_at_zero centres_without_demand weighted_mean
2 0.1030 2281 1 0.0401
3 0.0734 1804 1 0.0401
5 0.0502 1123 0 0.0405
8 0.0386 635 0 0.0405
10 0.0346 493 0 0.0405
15 0.0265 217 0 0.0405
NoteHow the code works
  • map_dfr() runs 2SFCA for each catchment size and stacks the one-row summaries. centres_without_demand counts the centres with no hexagon within d0. The capacity of those centres is lost in step 1, and the weighted mean falls below the ratio of supply to demand.

The standard deviation falls as the catchment grows, as Luo and Wang (2003) found. The share of hexagons with a 2SFCA score of 0 falls from 77% at 2 km to 7% at 15 km. With a 2 or 3 km catchment, one centre has no hexagon within the catchment. Its capacity is lost, so the weighted mean is below the ratio of supply to demand. That centre, with postal code 370093, has no hexagon within 3 km by road, although the centroid of hexagon 2479 is 125 m away in a straight line (map below).

On the street map, the eldercare centre and the centroid of hexagon 2479 are in the same housing estate, north of the Pan-Island Expressway. The centre and the centroid are connected by footpaths and Pipit Road. The exit_cost of the centre, from the nearest road to the centre, is 19 m, and the road closest to the centre on the street map is the expressway. An exit_cost of 19 m and a network_cost of 5,535 m are consistent with a network analysis that joined the centre to the expressway, so that the route to the centre runs along the expressway.

Of the 436 pairs of hexagon and centre less than 500 m apart in a straight line in the whole matrix, 69 are more than 2 km apart by road.

4.5 Demand: residents aged 65 and over by areal weighting

In section 2.3.3, every hexagon was given a demand of 100. According to the chapter, the actual demand should be used in practice. Kalogirou and Foley (2006) measured the demand for hospitals by the population aged 65 and over, as “the population sub-group who would be most likely to be the heaviest users”. Luo and Wang (2003) and Luo and Qi (2009) took the demand from census counts of the population. Polzin et al. (2014) adjusted the census counts with a health needs index that includes the share of the population under 15 and over 65. In this exercise, the demand for eldercare is measured by the residents aged 65 and over, as in Kalogirou and Foley (2006).

Exercise 1 used the 2020 census table of residents by subzone, age and sex from SingStat. The census counts residents by subzone, and the measures require a count for each hexagon. Areal weighting divides the count of each subzone among the hexagons in proportion to the area of the subzone that each hexagon covers. The method assumes that the residents are spread evenly over each subzone.

The question for this section is how much the accessibility scores change when the demand is the number of residents aged 65 and over in each hexagon.

popdata <- read_csv("data/aspatial/respop_census2020_agesex.csv",
                    col_types = cols(.default = "c"))

to_count <- function(x) {
  x <- str_replace_all(x, ",", "")
  x[x == "-"] <- "0"
  as.numeric(x)
}

aged_sz <- popdata |>
  mutate(across(-Number, to_count)) |>
  filter(!str_detect(toupper(Number), "^TOTAL$| ?- ?TOTAL$")) |>
  mutate(SUBZONE_N = toupper(str_trim(Number)),
         SUBZONE_N = if_else(str_starts(SUBZONE_N, "LAKESIDE"), "LAKESIDE", SUBZONE_N),
         AGED = Total_65_69 + Total_70_74 + Total_75_79 +
                Total_80_84 + Total_85_89 + Total_90andOver) |>
  group_by(SUBZONE_N) |>
  summarise(AGED = sum(AGED))

c(census_total = sum(aged_sz$AGED),
  matched_to_mp14 = sum(aged_sz$AGED[aged_sz$SUBZONE_N %in% mpsz$SUBZONE_N]))
   census_total matched_to_mp14 
         614900          614860
NoteHow the code works
  • col_types = cols(.default = "c") reads every column as text. As in Exercise 1, SingStat writes a nil or suppressed count as -. to_count() removes thousands separators, turns - into 0 and converts the text to numbers.
  • The table has a row for the whole country, a row for each planning area (its name ends in ” - Total”), and a row for each subzone. The regular expression drops the row for the whole country and the planning-area rows. One planning-area row is written “Changi- Total”, without the space, and " ?- ?TOTAL$" matches it as well.
  • The census of 2020 uses the subzones of the 2019 Master Plan, and the boundaries on this page are those of the 2014 Master Plan. The census subzones “Lakeside (Business)” and “Lakeside (Leisure)” are one subzone, “Lakeside”, in the 2014 plan, and their counts are added together.
  • AGED is the sum of the six age bands from 65 upwards.

The census counts 614,900 residents aged 65 and over. All but 40 of them live in subzones whose names appear in the 2014 boundaries. The other 40 residents live in Murai and Nicoll, two subzones of the 2019 plan with no subzone of the same name in the 2014 plan.

aged_poly <- mpsz |>
  left_join(aged_sz, by = "SUBZONE_N") |>
  mutate(AGED = replace_na(AGED, 0)) |>
  select(AGED)

hexagons$aged <- st_interpolate_aw(aged_poly, hexagons,
                                   extensive = TRUE)$AGED

c(aged_in_hexagons = sum(hexagons$aged),
  hexagons_without_aged = sum(hexagons$aged == 0))
     aged_in_hexagons hexagons_without_aged 
             613573.3                1334.0
NoteHow the code works 
st_interpolate_aw(x, to, extensive = TRUE)                # sf
  • st_interpolate_aw() intersects the subzones with the hexagons, and assigns each piece the share of the subzone’s count equal to its share of the subzone’s area. extensive = TRUE treats the count as a total to be divided among the pieces. The pieces of each hexagon are then added up. The result has one row per hexagon, in the order of hexagons.

The hexagons contain 99.8% of the residents aged 65 and over. The remaining residents live in the parts of subzones that the hexagons do not cover, on the offshore islands and along the coast. In total, 1,334 hexagons have no resident aged 65 and over, because they are in subzones with none: the water catchment areas, the airport, the industrial estates of the west and the port.

With this demand, SAM divides by zero in those hexagons:

p_aged <- hexagons$aged[ok]
sam_aged <- ac(p_aged, n100, D, power = 2, family = "SAM")
c(infinite = sum(is.infinite(sam_aged)),
  hexagons_with_aged = sum(p_aged > 0))
          infinite hexagons_with_aged 
              1218               1748

KD2SFCA with the kernel of Cheng et al. (2016) does not divide by the demand of the hexagon itself. A hexagon with no demand adds nothing to the denominator of the first step. In the second step, it has the score of the centres around it. With a capacity of 1 for each centre, the score is the number of centres per resident aged 65 and over within 5 km, weighted by the kernel and multiplied by 10,000:

kd_aged <- fca(p_aged, rep(1, length(n100)), D, "cheng") * 1e4

c(national_ratio = 1e4 * length(n100) / sum(p_aged),
  weighted_mean = weighted.mean(kd_aged, p_aged))
national_ratio  weighted_mean 
      1.962943       1.962943

The mean of the hexagon scores, weighted by demand, is 1.96 centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and over, which equals the national ratio, as Luo and Wang (2003) predict.

The scores range from 0 to 8.1 centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and over. Among the planning areas with more than 5,000 residents aged 65 and over, the table lists the five with the lowest and the five with the highest weighted mean score:

pa_summary <- tibble(planning_area = st_join(hexagons, mpsz["PLN_AREA_N"],
                                             join = st_intersects,
                                             largest = TRUE)$PLN_AREA_N[ok],
                     aged = p_aged, acc = kd_aged) |>
  group_by(planning_area) |>
  summarise(per_10k_aged = weighted.mean(acc, aged),
            aged_65 = round(sum(aged))) |>
  filter(aged_65 > 5000) |>
  arrange(per_10k_aged)

bind_rows(head(pa_summary, 5), tail(pa_summary, 5)) |>
  kable(digits = 2)
planning_area per_10k_aged aged_65

PASIR RIS 0.40 15303
BUKIT PANJANG 0.61 16289
HOUGANG 0.97 35659
SERANGOON 0.98 23579
GEYLANG 2.71 21163
QUEENSTOWN 2.86 18448
TOA PAYOH 3.25 24476
KALLANG 3.90 20972
BUKIT MERAH 5.43 32528
NoteHow the code works
  • Each hexagon is assigned to the planning area it overlaps most, as in section 4.6. The score of a planning area is the mean of the scores of its hexagons, weighted by their residents aged 65 and over. head() and tail() keep the five planning areas with the lowest scores and the five with the highest.
  • Map
  • Code
pa_named <- bind_rows(head(pa_summary, 5), tail(pa_summary, 5))
pa_lab <- label_areas(pa_named$planning_area) |>
  left_join(pa_named, by = c(PLN_AREA_N = "planning_area")) |>
  mutate(label = sprintf("%s %.2f", str_to_title(PLN_AREA_N), per_10k_aged))
tm_shape(hexagons, bbox = mapex) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "grey85", col_alpha = 0) +
tm_shape(mutate(hex_ok, kd_aged = kd_aged)) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "kd_aged",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
                breaks = c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 4, 6, 10, Inf) * nat_ratio / 2,
                values = "brewer.rd_yl_bu", midpoint = nat_ratio),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Centres per 10,000\nresidents aged 65+"),
              col_alpha = 0) +
tm_shape(eldercare) +
  tm_dots(size = 0.15, fill = "black") +
tm_shape(pa_lab) +
  tm_borders(col = "black", lwd = 1.2) +
  tm_labels("label", size = 0.7, fontface = "bold", bgcol = "white", bgcol_alpha = 0.85,
            options = opt_tm_labels(point.label = TRUE)) +
  tm_title("KD2SFCA (Cheng et al. kernel, 5 km), demand = residents aged 65 and over") +
  tm_layout(frame = FALSE, legend.outside = TRUE)
NoteHow the code works
  • The labelled planning areas are the ten of the table, with the score of each.
  • The class breaks are multiples of the national ratio, from 0 to 5 times, with the midpoint of the diverging palette at the national ratio. Red hexagons have a score below the national ratio, and blue hexagons a score above it.

The highest scores are in Bukit Merah, Kallang and Toa Payoh, near the city centre, with 5.4, 3.9, 3.2 centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and over. Sembawang, Pasir Ris and Bukit Panjang have scores of 0.28, 0.4, 0.61, below a third of the national ratio of 1.96.

The rank correlation between the scores under the census demand and the scores under a constant demand, over the 1,843 hexagons with a score above 0, is 0.98: the ranking of the hexagons is almost unchanged. The ratios \(R_j\) of the centres change more, with a rank correlation of 0.64 between the census demand and the constant demand. The ratio of a centre is its capacity divided by the weighted demand in its catchment, so a centre with many residents aged 65 and over within 5 km has a lower ratio under the census demand than under a constant demand.

4.6 Regional aggregation: one region per hexagon and population weights

In section 3, the regions were compared with boxplots of the hexagon scores, after a join by st_intersects that counts a hexagon in every subzone it touches. Long (2017, section 4) describes the aggregation of accessibility to regions, and warns that the aggregation is subject to the ecological fallacy and the modifiable areal unit problem. Luo and Wang (2003) weight the average of the accessibility scores by population. Luo and Qi (2009, Table 1) count the population of the areas whose ratio is below the shortage standard of 1 physician per 3,500 residents. The readings contain no shortage standard for eldercare centres. The threshold in this exercise, half the national ratio of centres to residents aged 65 and over, is an extension of the course material.

The question for this section is how the five regions compare when each hexagon counts once, and each resident aged 65 and over counts equally.

hexagons$REGION_N <- st_join(hexagons, mpsz["REGION_N"],
                             join = st_intersects, largest = TRUE)$REGION_N
nrow(hexagons)
[1] 3125
NoteHow the code works
  • largest = TRUE keeps, for each hexagon, only the subzone it overlaps most, so the join returns one row per hexagon.
eldercare$REGION_N <- st_join(eldercare, mpsz["REGION_N"])$REGION_N

region_summary <- tibble(region = hexagons$REGION_N[ok],
                         aged = p_aged,
                         acc = kd_aged,
                         reach = colSums(t(D) <= 5) > 0) |>
  group_by(region) |>
  summarise(hexagons = n(),
            aged_65 = round(sum(aged)),
            per_10k_aged = weighted.mean(acc, aged),
            aged_no_centre_5km = sum(aged[!reach]) / sum(aged),
            aged_below_half_national = sum(aged[acc < nat_ratio / 2]) / sum(aged)) |>
  left_join(count(st_drop_geometry(eldercare), REGION_N, name = "centres"),
            by = c(region = "REGION_N"))

kable(region_summary, digits = 3)
region hexagons aged_65 per_10k_aged aged_no_centre_5km aged_below_half_national centres
CENTRAL REGION 575 181475 3.261 0.007 0.124 61
EAST REGION 488 107456 1.333 0.006 0.323 13
NORTH REGION 609 65843 1.383 0.065 0.400 9
NORTH-EAST REGION 319 131771 1.300 0.007 0.340 17
WEST REGION 975 124782 1.624 0.041 0.291 20
NoteHow the code works
  • reach is TRUE for a hexagon with at least one centre within 5 km by road. t() transposes the matrix, one column per hexagon, so colSums(t(D) <= 5) counts the centres within 5 km of each hexagon.
  • per_10k_aged is the mean score of the region weighted by the residents aged 65 and over in each hexagon. aged_no_centre_5km and aged_below_half_national are the shares of the region’s residents aged 65 and over who live in hexagons with no centre within 5 km, and in hexagons with a score below half the national ratio.

The Central Region has 61 of the 120 centres, and a score of 3.3 centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and over. In the other four regions, the score is between 1.3 and 1.6, below the national ratio of 1.96. The North-East Region has the lowest score, with 131,771 residents aged 65 and over, the second-largest number of the five regions, and 17 centres. In the North Region, 6.5% of the residents aged 65 and over live more than 5 km by road from a centre, and 40% live in hexagons with a score below half the national ratio. Both shares are the largest of the five regions.

tibble(region = hexagons$REGION_N[ok], aged = p_aged, acc = kd_aged) |>
  filter(aged >= 1) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = region, y = acc, weight = aged)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "grey90") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = nat_ratio, colour = "red", linetype = "dashed") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "centres per 10,000 residents aged 65+ (log scale)",
       subtitle = "Hexagons with at least one resident aged 65+, weighted by that number; dashed line: national ratio") +
  theme_minimal()
NoteHow the code works
  • aes(weight = aged) weights each hexagon by its residents aged 65 and over, so that each hexagon counts in proportion to its residents aged 65 and over. A hexagon with two such residents has a weight of 2, and a hexagon in a housing estate a weight of several hundred.
  • scale_y_log10() puts the scores on a logarithmic scale. The 119 hexagons with residents aged 65 and over and a score of 0 have no logarithm, and are left out of the boxes.

In this chart, each hexagon appears once. The regions are compared by one score, in centres per 10,000 residents aged 65 and over. The dashed line marks the national ratio, which is the score every region would have if the centres were distributed in proportion to the residents aged 65 and over.

5 Reflection

In chapter 17, accessibility to eldercare centres is modelled with three measures from one function. The three maps of Part 1 show the same pattern: high scores in the city centre and around each eldercare centre, and low scores in the west, the reservoir areas and the far east. In Part 2, I found that the scores depend on the distance matrix, the formula inside ac(), the size of the catchment and the demand.

The distance matrix has errors. 159 hexagons have one distance to all 120 centres, the distance to the last centre in the file. One of them is within 5 km of every centre in the matrix. Under 2SFCA, it was the highest-scoring hexagon until I removed the 159 hexagons. The other 158 hexagons score 0 under KD2SFCA in Part 1. Of the 159 hexagons, 94 hexagons have a centre within 5 km in a straight line, so their scores of 0 come from wrong distances. I found the errors by comparing the network distances with straight-line distances. Some valid distances are also much longer than the straight line: centre 370093 is 125 m from hexagon 2479 in a straight line and 5.6 km away by road. With a catchment of 2 or 3 km, its capacity is lost.

Three measures of ac() differ from the formulas on the slides and in the readings. Its Hansen measure uses an exponential decay, where Hansen (1959) used a power of distance. When the capacities of the centres differ, the Hansen measure also multiplies the weights of one centre by the capacity of another centre. Its KD2SFCA kernel has no width. With distances in kilometres, the weights beyond 2 km are below 0.02, so a catchment of 5 km has the effect of a catchment of about 2 km. The KD2SFCA scores also change with the unit of distance. Its SAM does not use d0. It uses the demand once, where the formula on slide 29 uses it twice. With a constant demand, its SAM equals a Hansen measure with the power function \(1/d^2\), divided by the demand. None of these differences appears in the chapter’s output. I found each difference by reading the source of ac(), which is about 50 lines long.

The floating catchment scores are a capacity per person. The unit is the same for 2SFCA, E2SFCA and KD2SFCA. The mean of their scores weighted by demand equals the national ratio, a property derived by Luo and Wang (2003). Every computation of these methods with a catchment of 5 km or more satisfies the property. With a catchment of 2 or 3 km, one centre has no hexagon within its catchment, and the mean falls below the ratio. The Hansen and SAM scores have no unit. They can be compared only as ranks or ratios between hexagons, as Long (2017) says of gravity-based measures.

The demand changes the ratios of the centres more than the scores of the hexagons. With the residents aged 65 and over in place of a constant demand of 100, the rank correlation is 0.98 for the hexagon scores and 0.64 for the centre ratios.

Regions under the census demand. With the KD2SFCA kernel of Cheng et al. (2016), the score of every region outside the Central Region is below the national ratio. The North-East Region has the lowest score. In the North Region, 6.5% of the residents aged 65 and over have no centre within 5 km by road, the largest share of the five regions.

Limits. Every centre has a capacity of 100, because the data have no measure of the size of a centre. Areal weighting spreads the residents of a subzone evenly over its area, including its parks and industrial land. The census is from 2020. The records of the centres were last updated in July 2016, according to the field FMEL_UPD_D of the shapefile. The chapter gives no information on the road network used for OD_Matrix.csv. I took the catchment of 5 km and the kernels from the chapter and the readings, without data on how far residents aged 65 and over in Singapore travel to a centre.

7 About this document

Written and executed in Quarto with R 4.6.1, SpatialAcc 0.1.6, sf 1.1.2 and tmap 4.4.1. All figures and tables are generated at render time from the data in data/, so nothing on this page is pasted in.

I used AI assistance while working out the approach and the extensions in Part 2. The analysis was run and checked by me.
